summary:
The department of Vaupés stands under the national framework of Colombia, whose formal legal framework is among the most developed in the region. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015; the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry ordered all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (a hotel), T-909 of 2011 (mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, but no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025; 41 trans women were killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. The bearing on Vaupés is that lethal anti-trans violence has occurred in daylight, been filmed, and left the perpetrator unarrested.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed actors. In Caquetá department, flyers on the street and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Discrimination limits trans women in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising.
tangentialFactors:
The violent incidents documented here occurred in Antioquia and Caquetá, not in Vaupés. They are cited as national context rather than as findings about the department: the pattern they establish is that armed groups run territorial campaigns of threats and displacement against named trans women, and that such campaigns have in other departments driven trans women out of their homes at short notice.

Colombia's legal protections and its lived conditions diverge sharply, a gap the UN Independent Expert described in May 2025 as a disconnect between institutional progress and daily experience. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, reported as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Work and economic options are a compounding factor: discrimination restricts trans women in the documented department mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which shapes exposure to street-level and armed-group violence.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since the rule change approved in June 2015 and supported by Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognising self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Same-sex couples married abroad present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office to obtain the same visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses; the National Registry has instructed all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a trans-specific legal, enforcement or violence finding inside Vaupés itself. Whether the armed-group flyer and kill-list campaigns documented in Caquetá and Guajira operate in Vaupés is unresolved on the present sources, as is the department's own homicide record for trans people.

The arrest status of those responsible for the killing of Sara Millerey was unresolved as of the 14 April 2025 report: police had interrogated local residents and the president had ordered an urgent investigation, but no arrests had been made.

The legislative status of a comprehensive trans law is not covered by the sources assembled here and remains unresolved. So does the practical availability of notary-based marker changes in Vaupés's more remote municipalities, which no source addresses.
